title: The veterans benefits office lost my grandfather's file for four years. When we demanded a supervisor, we found out why (PART 2)

blocks.text: He didn't actually lock us in. He asked us, very politely, to stay in the conference room while he made two phone calls. My grandfather, who'd served two tours in Vietnam, sat with his hands folded on his cane and said, "Son, I've waited four years. I can wait another hour."

Within that hour, two agents from the Office of Inspector General arrived from the federal building across the street. They spent the afternoon with the supervisor, copying records. Before we left, one of them knelt beside my grandfather's chair, shook his hand, and said, "Thank you for not giving up."

It took four months for the full story to come out. A claims processor in that office had been quietly marking certain veterans' files as "resolved" and redirecting their retroactive back-pay vouchers into a dormant government holding account.

From there, she'd filed fake invoices from a shell company she'd set up under her cousin's name and paid them out of that account. She chose veterans who were elderly, lived alone, or had no family members calling to check on them.
The processor and her cousin were charged with federal theft and wire fraud. The office brought in an outside team to review every "resolved" claim from the last six years.
My grandfather received his full back pay: four years of disability benefits, plus interest. It was enough to cover every prescription he'd struggled to pay for, with plenty left over.
The first thing he did was buy back his old truck.
The man he'd sold it to, a neighbor down the road, sold it back to him for exactly what he'd paid. When he heard the story, he threw in a full tank of gas.

Now my grandfather drives to the VFW every Thursday and tells the younger veterans the same thing: "Keep copies of everything. And if something's taking too long, bring your grandkid and sit in the lobby."
